h.strategy: Obvious hypotheses (an edit matters more when an alternative path is removed; strong components help more when connected) score zero even if true. Target effects that real measurements often show but intuition misses: ceiling effects (a normally helpful edit helps less, or hurts, when the parent is already strong); redundancy (two strong components in parallel are worth less than either alone suggests); substitution (a cheap or 'weak' option beats a strong one when capacity elsewhere is high); and sign reversals of an edit's usual effect under specific conditions. Each hypothesis needs a concrete mechanism. Vary the edited field and the conditioning field across hypotheses, and include both HIGHER and LOWER directions.

hyps.why: When a strong conv path feeds the output already, a cheap pooled direct edge costs little and can even regularize.
When the conv work is done upstream, pooling on the final edge is a cheap substitute that hurts much less than usual.
With a strong conv on the parallel stem edge, a pooled edge 0 costs little and adds multi-scale smoothing.
A conv-processed node 1 feeding the output via identity combines deep features with a shortcut.
Identity from node 1 to 2 lets conv-heavy output edges operate on both raw and processed features, rather than stacking more depth.
Without the direct edge, a skip on the last edge restores a residual route to the output, which matters more than usual.
When later edges carry strong convs, a cheap 1x1 stem loses little relative to conv3x3, so the substitution is better tolerated.
With the node-1 path cut, the direct edge is the main route, so a learnable 1x1 there helps more than usual.
Removing the direct edge costs less when a strong conv path exists, since the shortcut's role is partly redundant.
With edge 0 removed, node 1 receives no signal, so a conv on edge 1→3 is inert and gives none of its usual gain.
